I define property as anything that's valuable that isn't a human being. This could include portable property (money, cars, precious metals, etc.), real estate, and intellectual property.

Property is a social construct. It is not something that exists in nature or the laws of physics. It is your right to claim control over something insofar as that right is agreed to and defended by the rest of society up to the point of violent force, except where you have some independent ability to defend that right by your own force, which is usually very weak. The conditions we accept upon this construct vary with the dominant cultural, economic, and moral philosophies. One might attribute a high degree of propriety to the products of personal labor. Yet we don't attribute very high value to that on a labor market and do not consider the factory worker to have any vested interest in the products of his labor as long as he's paid for it. Conditions are also situational. The needs of the many usually outweigh the needs of the few in a crisis. We usually consider those who hoard in a crisis to be acting immorally--or at the very least amorally--and those who steal when they're starving or break into an empty building or home in search shelter in a disaster situation somewhat justified and forgivable in breaking those usual mores given the situation. Such social constructs should never be treated as moral absolutes. There are no moral absolutes--and shouldn't be.

The 'tragedy of the commons' has been well debunked by many because it has rarely, if ever, actually occurred in history and presumes a kind of over-simplistic pathological behavior that doesn't normally exist among responsible adults. The actual tragedy of the commons is its systematic and global capture and enclosure into private property as a means to engineer scarcity.
